newsitem.title: THAILAND: Japan car companies aim to keep ASEAN dominance.
newsitem.headline: Japan car companies aim to keep ASEAN dominance.

text.p: Japanese car companies said they would strive to retain their dominance of auto industry markets in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) region well into the next century.
The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) made the statement in a paper distributed at the first conference on ASEAN Auto Supporting Industries on Wednesday.

Toshiaki Yasuda, JAMA chief representative, said Japanese auto makers produced 1.1 million vehicles through their wholly owned or joint venture assembly plants in ASEAN last year, up 25 percent from 1995 and four times of their production in 1985.

Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO) said in a report for the meeting that ASEAN's car output is projected to rise to about 2.39 million vehicles annually by the year 2000 from about 1.34 million in 1995.
It said Thai automobile production will likely increase to 1.04 million vehicles a year from 526,000 during the same period.

"ASEAN automobile industries are riding the wave of motorisation in the region caused by economic development and are steadily growing in terms of both production and markets. By the 21st century, production is expected to double," JETRO said.
About 1,500 representatives of auto and car parts producers mostly from Japan, ASEAN members, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar attended the two-day conference hosted by JAMA and JETRO.
ASEAN groups Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand and Vietnam.
Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Industry Minister Korn Dabbaransi told the meeting ASEAN would be the world biggest auto production centre by the turn of the century.
"By the turn of the century, all leading automobile companies will set up their final assembly plants in ASEAN countries," he said.

The minister said he would push for more Thai government incentives for the auto industry, including new free trade zones for car makers and elimination of bureaucratic redtape that inflation their production cost.

"We want to make your FOB cost as low as possible...by eliminating customs redtape...We don't want to hear that you have high cost problems because of our bureaucracy," he told Japanese and ASEAN auto parts manufacturers.
